originalTitle: College can cost $100,000 a year. Here's how families are covering the tab
summary: Because families struggle to pay for school, many students and their parents increasingly depend on federal and private aid to help foot the bill.
content:
With a growing number of colleges and universities costing more than $100,000 a year, higher education is slipping out of reach for many students, several reports now show.

Just 12% of surveyed Americans say four-year colleges are affordable, according to a recent Lumina Foundation and Gallup poll , which surveyed 14,000 adults without a degree or who are working toward one, nearly 6,000 college graduates, and 2,000 employers June 1-15. Cost is the single biggest barrier to entry for prospective students, an earlier Lumina Foundation and Gallup release from the same study said.

"Americans haven't given up on higher education; they want it for their children ... but they are questioning whether they can afford it," said Courtney Brown, chief data and research officer for the Lumina Foundation, which is aimed at improving higher education access.

Because so many families struggle to cover the tab, they have increasingly depended on federal and private aid to help foot the bill.

How students and families finance college

Nearly half of families borrowed money to pay for college in the 2025-26 academic year, and 68% of those respondents said borrowing was always part of their plan, according to Sallie Mae's new How America Pays for College report. The survey polled 1,000 parents of undergraduate students between the ages of 18 and 24, as well as 1,000 undergraduate students, in April and May.

In most cases, parent income and savings cover less than half of college costs. Free money from scholarships and grants accounts for more than a quarter of the costs, and student loans make up most of the rest, the education lender found.

Despite the growing debt burden, families have continued to take out loans at a fairly consistent rate, according to Sallie spokesman Rick Castellano. However, "if you are going to borrow for school, the last thing you want to do is overborrow — and ultimately, you want to have a plan for how you'll pay it back," he said.

Read more CNBC personal finance coverage

A separate survey by College Ave found that savings alone play a smaller role in education funding and families are relying on a broader mix of sources to make college possible — including savings, student employment, federal and private student loans, and credit cards . The private student loan company polled 1,000 parents of current college students at four-year institutions in June.

In 2026, parents who saved for college reported having set aside $37,897, a significant decline from the $51,310 they reported in 2025, according to College Ave.

As a result, just 16% of families who saved for college said they felt prepared to cover the total cost of a degree through savings alone, down from 27% a year earlier.

The findings come as families face new limits on federal student loans. Starting this year, the legislation established in President Donald Trump 's "big beautiful bill" caps the amount students can borrow.

Two-thirds — 66% — of families surveyed support limits on federal student borrowing, Sallie Mae's report found.

"We'll see how that plays out over the next year," Castellano said. "It will be interesting to see if it changes how students and families approach school choice — we know they are looking at costs just as well as academics."

Except for buying a home , a college education is now the largest expense an individual is likely to have in a lifetime.

It wasn't always like that. In recent decades, deep cuts in state funding have contributed to sharp tuition increases and transferred more of the cost of college to students and their families, according to analyses by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan research group based in Washington, D.C.

Tuition had historically risen about 3% a year, according to the College Board . But during the Great Recession, declining state investment caused tuition to skyrocket. At private four-year schools, average tuition and fees rose 26% from 2008 to 2018. Tuition plus fees at four-year public schools, which were harder hit, jumped 35% over the same period.

The recession caused by the Covid pandemic led to a new round of cuts to public colleges and universities, the CBPP found.

Today, tuition accounts for about half of college revenue, while state and local governments provide the other half. But the split used to be much different, with tuition providing just about a quarter of revenue and state and local governments picking up the rest.

Because colleges receive less financial support from states and are more reliant on tuition revenue, college tuition costs have increased much faster than any other household expense, according to a 2026 report by J.P. Morgan Asset Management , based on data through the end of 2025.

As schools spend more to hire faculty, make capital improvements and attract students, tuition is rising about 5.5% a year , outpacing inflation and wage gains, J.P. Morgan Asset Management found.

At that rate, "I wouldn't be surprised if we see more students and families thinking about cost and the ROI of earning a degree," Castellano said. "You want to get the most value out of what is a significant investment."
chineseTitle: 大学一年费用可能为 100,000 美元。以下是家庭如何支付账单
chineseSummary: 由于家庭难以支付学费，许多学生及其家长越来越依赖联邦和私人援助来支付账单。
chineseContent:
现在有几份报告显示，随着越来越多的学院和大学每年的学费超过 10 万美元，高等教育对许多学生来说正在变得遥不可及。

Lumina 基金会和盖洛普最近的一项民意调查显示，只有 12% 的受访美国人表示四年制大学是负担得起的。该民意调查于 6 月 1 日至 15 日对 14,000 名没有学位或正在为一个人工作的成年人、近 6,000 名大学毕业生和 2,000 名雇主进行了调查。 Lumina 基金会和盖洛普早些时候发布的同一项研究称，成本是潜在学生入学的最大障碍。

旨在改善高等教育机会的卢米纳基金会首席数据和研究官考特尼·布朗表示：“美国人并没有放弃高等教育；他们希望自己的孩子能够接受高等教育……但他们质疑自己是否负担得起。”

由于许多家庭难以支付账单，他们越来越依赖联邦和私人援助来帮助支付账单。

学生和家庭如何资助大学费用

根据萨莉·梅 (Sallie Mae) 最新的《美国如何支付大学费用》报告，近一半的家庭在 2025-26 学年借钱支付大学费用，其中 68% 的受访者表示，借贷始终是他们计划的一部分。该调查于 4 月和 5 月对 1,000 名 18 岁至 24 岁之间的本科生家长以及 1,000 名本科生进行了调查。

在大多数情况下，父母的收入和储蓄只够支付大学费用的不到一半。这家教育贷款机构发现，来自奖学金和助学金的免费资金占成本的四分之一以上，而学生贷款则占其余大部分。

萨利发言人里克·卡斯特拉诺表示，尽管债务负担不断增加，但家庭仍继续以相当稳定的利率申请贷款。然而，“如果你要为学校借贷，你最不想做的就是过度借贷——最终，你想要制定一个如何偿还贷款的计划，”他说。

阅读更多 CNBC 个人理财报道

College Ave 的另一项调查发现，仅储蓄在教育经费中发挥的作用较小，家庭依靠更广泛的来源来上大学，包括储蓄、学生就业、联邦和私人学生贷款以及信用卡。这家私人学生贷款公司 6 月份对 1,000 名四年制院校在校大学生家长进行了调查。

根据College Ave.的数据，2026年，为大学储蓄的家长报告说他们存了37,897美元，比他们报告的2025年的51,310美元显着下降。

因此，在为大学存钱的家庭中，只有 16% 表示他们准备通过储蓄来支付学位的总费用，低于一年前的 27%。

这一调查结果发布之际，家庭面临联邦学生贷款的新限制。从今年开始，唐纳德·特朗普总统的“美丽大法案”中制定的立法限制了学生可以借贷的金额。

Sallie Mae 的报告发现，三分之二（66%）的受访家庭支持限制联邦学生借贷。

“我们将在明年看看情况如何，”卡斯特拉诺说。 “看看它是否会改变学生和家庭选择学校的方式将会很有趣——我们知道他们在考虑成本的同时也考虑了学业。”

除了买房之外，大学教育现在是一个人一生中可能花费的最大开支。

情况并非总是如此。总部位于华盛顿特区的无党派研究组织预算和政策优先事项中心的分析显示，近几十年来，国家资金的大幅削减导致学费大幅上涨，并将更多的大学费用转移给学生及其家庭。

根据大学理事会的数据，学费历来每年上涨约 3%。但在大衰退期间，国家投资下降导致学费飙升。 2008年至2018年，私立四年制学校的平均学杂费上涨了26%。受打击最严重的四年制公立学校的学杂费同期上涨了35%。

CBPP 发现，新冠疫情造成的经济衰退导致公立学院和大学进行新一轮的削减。

如今，学费约占大学收入的一半，而州和地方政府提供另一半。但过去的分配情况却大不相同，学费仅提供约四分之一的收入，州和地方政府则承担其余部分。

摩根大通资产管理公司根据截至 2025 年底的数据发布的 2026 年报告显示，由于大学获得的州财政支持较少，并且更加依赖学费收入，因此大学学费的增长速度远远快于任何其他家庭支出。

摩根大通资产管理公司发现，随着学校花更多的钱聘请教师、改善资本和吸引学生，学费每年上涨约 5.5%，超过了通货膨胀和工资涨幅。

按照这个速度，“如果我们看到更多的学生和家庭考虑获得学位的成本和投资回报率，我不会感到惊讶，”卡斯特拉诺说。 “你希望从一项重大投资中获得最大价值。”
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于财经市场信号，适合用于观察利率、汇率、股债商品、金融机构和宏观政策变化。
